classification.difficultyReason: Identify opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to theta, then substitute into the six taught ratio definitions.

questions.mappingNote: This question directly repeats Example 1's six-ratio method with opposite 5, adjacent 12 and hypotenuse 13. Define the trigonometric ratios is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines all six side ratios and demonstrates direct substitution in a right triangle; page 2 retains the reciprocal circular-function definitions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse and evaluate their six ratios from supplied side lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Find an unlabelled hypotenuse and evaluate all six ratios exactly.

questions.mappingNote: This acute-angle triangle uses the side-ratio method of Example 1; its missing hypotenuse is obtained by Pythagoras before evaluating the six functions.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 defines all six ratios from opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse and evaluates them in Example 1. Page 2 connects these ratios with circular functions and states the reciprocal definitions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find an unlabelled hypotenuse and evaluate all six ratios exactly.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent each cardinal rotation on a unit circle and associate the endpoint coordinates with the supplied sine and cosine values.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts request unit-circle illustrations of supplied cardinal-angle values, directly assessing unit-circle definitions rather than numerical evaluation.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines sine as the unit-circle endpoint's y-coordinate and cosine as its x-coordinate, with positive angles measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Illustrate supplied sine and cosine values at the four cardinal angles using unit-circle coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Intersect the quadrant sign conditions; the hardest part first translates secant and cotangent signs into cosine and sine signs.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses the signs of unit-circle coordinates and their ratios. Unit-circle definitions is the closest catalogue skill; tangent as sine over cosine supports the mixed-sign parts.
questions.methodNote: Use the unit-circle quadrant signs for sine, cosine and tangent; use secant and cotangent definitions to infer the corresponding signs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify quadrants from the signs of circular functions, including reciprocal functions.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite reciprocal and quotient functions in sine and cosine, simplify division of fractions, and identify the remaining ratio.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess simplification using the supplied definitions, so simplify-trig-expressions is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the six right-triangle ratio definitions on page 1 and the circular and reciprocal function definitions on page 2. Replace tangent, cotangent, secant and cosecant by expressions in sine and cosine, cancel factors, then identify the resulting ratio.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution of the circular-function and reciprocal definitions followed by cancellation.

classification.difficultyReason: Find acute reference angles in different quadrants, including negative angles and angles exceeding one revolution.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 establishes positive and negative rotations; page 4 defines and illustrates reference angles; page 5 demonstrates their use. The selected catalogue skill is the closest match for finding reference angles in degrees.
questions.methodNote: Use coterminal angles and the acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis. In Quadrants II, III and IV use 180°−θ, θ−180° and 360°−θ respectively.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find acute reference angles in different quadrants, including negative angles and angles exceeding one revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Find acute reference angles in radians, including negative angles and angles exceeding one revolution.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill is exact-ratios-radians: these parts assess its prerequisite reference-angle reasoning for multiples of pi/6 and pi/4, without requesting function values.
questions.methodNote: Use a coterminal angle within one revolution, identify its quadrant, and find the acute reference angle using the unit-circle relationships demonstrated on pages 4 and 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find acute reference angles in radians, including negative angles and angles exceeding one revolution.

classification.difficultyReason: Devise an unsignposted comparison through cos(1), establishing sin(u)<u geometrically and using decreasing cosine to bound the two nested expressions on opposite sides.

questions.mappingNote: Unit-circle definitions are the closest catalogue skill for comparing nested circular functions; radian measure supports the side-versus-arc argument.
questions.methodNote: Use the unit-circle coordinate definitions, positive radian angles, and the geometric comparison of sine with arc length. The matched teacher solution supplies the sine inequality and decreasing-cosine argument.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires a no-calculator comparison of nested circular functions using unit-circle geometry and monotonicity.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the given cosine into the Pythagorean identity and retain both square roots because the quadrant is unspecified.

questions.mappingNote: Finding another ratio from a supplied ratio is the closest catalogue match; no quadrant is supplied.
questions.methodNote: Substitute into the Pythagorean identity and take both square roots, as in Example 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into the Pythagorean identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the Pythagorean identity to obtain cosine squared, simplify its square root, and retain both possible signs.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluate an unknown ratio from one given ratio.
questions.methodNote: Use the Pythagorean identity and retain both square roots.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct identity substitution with two possible signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Find both possible sine values using the Pythagorean identity, then divide by the given cosine to obtain tangent.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is evaluating a ratio from another ratio.
questions.methodNote: Use the Pythagorean identity, followed by tangent as sine divided by cosine.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find sine using the identity, then form the tangent quotient.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect the given tangent to a Pythagorean relation, recover cosine and then sine, preserving the two possible quadrant signs.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluate sine from a given tangent without a specified quadrant.
questions.methodNote: Use the derived secant–tangent identity and the sine/cosine quotient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use a reciprocal identity and preserve the undetermined sign.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert cosecant to sine, use the Pythagorean identity to find both cosine values, then take reciprocals for secant.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluate secant from a given cosecant.
questions.methodNote: Use reciprocal definitions and the Pythagorean identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert a reciprocal ratio and apply the Pythagorean identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert secant to cosine, find both sine values with the Pythagorean identity, and take reciprocals to obtain cosecant.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluate cosecant from one known ratio.
questions.methodNote: Use reciprocal definitions and both square roots in the Pythagorean identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert secant to cosine and find the reciprocal of sine.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the taught cosecant–cotangent identity, substitute the given value and retain both square roots.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluate cotangent from the given cosecant.
questions.methodNote: Apply the derived identity cotangent squared plus one equals cosecant squared.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into the cosecant–cotangent identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Replace tangent by sine over cosine, cancel the cosine factor and rewrite sine squared using the Pythagorean identity.

questions.mappingNote: The explicit task is proving an identity.
questions.methodNote: Transform the left-hand side using ratio definitions and the Pythagorean identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: A short proof using the tangent quotient and Pythagorean identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that squaring the sine–cosine sum exposes their product through the Pythagorean identity, then reverse this relationship while retaining both sum signs.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts evaluate combinations of ratios by identity-based algebra.
questions.methodNote: Expand the square and replace sine squared plus cosine squared with one.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand a squared sum and use the Pythagorean identity in both directions.

classification.difficultyReason: Reframe the tangent–cotangent sum as the reciprocal of the sine–cosine product, connect that product to the square of the requested sum, and select the positive root using acuteness.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task combines identities to evaluate a sum.
questions.methodNote: Reduce tangent and cotangent to sine and cosine, combine fractions, then use the Pythagorean identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine reciprocal ratios, obtain a product, then use a squared sum and the acute-angle sign.

classification.difficultyReason: Expand the three squares, recognise reciprocal cross-products as constants, and regroup the remaining terms into the three Pythagorean identities while managing the subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: The task is an identity proof involving all six ratios.
questions.methodNote: Expand the three squares separately, then use the original and both derived Pythagorean identities.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Expand three squared sums and combine all three Pythagorean identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the fourth-power difference as a difference of squares, use the Pythagorean identity on one factor and cancel the remaining terms.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluate an expression by identity-based simplification.
questions.methodNote: Use the difference-of-squares factorisation demonstrated in Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factor a difference of squares and simplify using the Pythagorean identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Reframe the sixth powers as cubes of sine squared and cosine squared, then connect a cubic factorisation or expansion to their sum being one.

questions.mappingNote: Simplification of a higher-power trigonometric expression is directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Combine algebraic factorisation with the Pythagorean identity, following the approach of Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a sum of cubes after substituting squared ratios and use their sum of one.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of cosine symmetry and periodicity to a supplied ratio.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 directly assesses cosine ratios for supplementary, negative and periodic angles. The quadrant-form skill is the closest supplied catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Apply the supplementary-angle identity, evenness of cosine and periodicity. Page 9 supplies the periodicity formulas and Example 1; page 10 supplies negative- and supplementary-angle formulas; the Example 3 continuation on page 11 demonstrates the same substitutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of cosine symmetry and periodicity to a supplied ratio.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into supplementary, negative-angle and periodicity identities.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c directly apply the formulas on pages 9–10. Part d first removes one full revolution, then applies the negative-angle formula. The selected catalogue skill is the closest match for quadrant-form identities expressed in radians.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied periodicity, supplementary-angle and negative-angle formulas; substitute the given sine value after applying the identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into supplementary, negative-angle and periodicity identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate tangent symmetry; the most involved angle requires periodic reduction followed by a sign change.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply the supplementary-angle and negative-angle formulas respectively; part c applies π periodicity; part d first removes 2π, then applies the supplementary-angle formula. The selected skill is the closest catalogue match for these quadrant-form identities in radians.
questions.methodNote: Use the periodicity formula tan(θ+2π)=tan θ and tan(θ+π)=tan θ from page 9, and the negative-angle and supplementary-angle tangent formulas from page 10.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of taught tangent symmetry and periodicity identities.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine complementary-angle identities with supplementary or periodic reductions, tracking the sign before substituting the supplied cosine value.

questions.mappingNote: Every part evaluates a sine expression from the supplied cosine value; complementary-trig-identities is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the complementary sine identity, supplementary-angle symmetry and sine periodicity. These are illustrated by the unit-circle teaching on pages 9–10 and complementary-angle formulas and Example 4 on page 11.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply complementary-angle identities together with supplementary-angle symmetry and periodicity.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply complementary angle identities together with supplementary angle signs and periodicity.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 evaluates cosine expressions from a given sine ratio. Parts a and b use complementary and supplementary angles; c adds a half-turn to b; d removes a full turn from a. Complementary angle identities are the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the complementary cosine identity on page 11, supplementary cosine identity on page 10, and cosine periodicity and half-turn sign change on page 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply complementary angle identities together with supplementary angle signs and periodicity.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply complementary-angle identities with negative angles and periodicity.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 directly assesses complementary identities for cotangent, extending them through negative angles and whole-period shifts.
questions.methodNote: Use the complementary identity cot(pi/2−θ)=tan θ from Example 4(c), the negative-angle tangent identity, and periodicity. Cotangent periodicity follows by taking reciprocals of the taught tangent periodicity identity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply complementary-angle identities with negative angles and periodicity.

classification.difficultyReason: Use complementary angle identities to rewrite both products, then apply the Pythagorean identity.

questions.mappingNote: The printed hint explicitly assesses complementary angle identities. Simplification using the Pythagorean identity is the supporting step.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 supplies the complementary angle formulas; page 10 demonstrates the Pythagorean identity. Rewrite the complementary ratios before combining the squared sine and cosine terms.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use complementary angle identities to rewrite both products, then apply the Pythagorean identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise complementary pairs in a 91-term sum and account separately for the central term.

questions.mappingNote: This question precedes the 19D topic band on page 12 and matches Section C question 8 in the teacher answers. Complementary trigonometric identities are the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the question's complementary-angle hint and the Pythagorean identity shown in Example 2 on page 10. Pair complementary angles, leaving the 45-degree term.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise complementary pairs in a 91-term sum and account separately for the central term.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise complementary-angle pairs across a product of 89 factors and handle the unpaired middle factor.

questions.mappingNote: Complementary trigonometric identities are directly assessed: tan of an angle and tan of its complement are reciprocals. The question precedes the 19D band and belongs to 19C.
questions.methodNote: Use complementary-angle symmetry to pair tangent factors, as explicitly demonstrated in the Section C question 9 teacher solution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise complementary-angle pairs across a product of 89 factors and handle the unpaired middle factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied angle-sum hint, halve the resulting expression and apply the taught complementary sine–cosine identity.

questions.mappingNote: This is Section C question 10, above the new 19D topic band. The assessed proof uses complementary angle identities rather than solving a trigonometric equation.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied triangle-angle-sum hint, then apply the complementary sine–cosine identity. The source question's hint and the Section C teacher solution explicitly support this sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines the triangle angle sum with the complementary sine–cosine identity to prove a general result.

classification.difficultyReason: Reduce reciprocal trigonometric expressions to sine, cosine or tangent, then find every solution in the stated degree interval.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (c) use reciprocal identities followed by reference angles; (b) also uses the complementary sine identity; (d) and (e) simplify reciprocal products before using quadrant signs. The restricted-domain skill is the closest primary catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 uses exact reference angles and quadrant signs on a restricted interval. Example 2 explicitly restricts the search to the stated interval. Example 3(b) rewrites tangent in sine and cosine before solving.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Reduce reciprocal trigonometric expressions to sine, cosine or tangent, then find every solution in the stated degree interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires periodicity, symmetry and a double-angle identity to obtain every solution on a closed interval.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) applies tangent periodicity; (b) and (c) apply equal-value symmetry and periodicity to compound arguments; (d) uses a double-angle identity followed by the factorisation method of Example 3. The inspected examples do not explicitly demonstrate the equal-value formulas or double-angle identity.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 use reference angles, quadrant signs, periodic rotation and transformed intervals. Example 3 uses substitution and factorisation to reduce equations to elementary trigonometric equations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Requires periodicity, symmetry and a double-angle identity to obtain every solution on a closed interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply vertical scaling and reflection to standard sine key points and distinguish the resulting curves on common axes.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 directly applies the amplitude discussion and reflected sine example.
questions.methodNote: Plot quarter-cycle key points; use amplitude and reflection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare vertical dilations and reflections of a standard sine curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Scale and reflect the standard cosine key points, preserving the period and placing each curve on common axes.

questions.mappingNote: The cosine table and amplitude rule supply the method for all six curves.
questions.methodNote: Plot quarter-cycle cosine points and apply amplitude/reflection.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare vertical dilations and reflections of a standard cosine curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Transform sine key points by vertical translations; the hardest curve combines amplitude scaling with a vertical shift before plotting.

questions.mappingNote: Example 1(a) combines a sine dilation with a vertical shift, as required by the third listed function.
questions.methodNote: Find amplitude, average, maximum, minimum and period; transform sine key points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare vertical shifts, including a simultaneous dilation and shift.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the standard cosine curve vertically by each supplied constant while retaining its amplitude, period and horizontal key-point positions.

questions.mappingNote: The vertical-shift rule explicitly applies to cosine.
questions.methodNote: Translate the standard cosine key points vertically.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare four vertical translations with a standard cosine curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret each internal subtraction as a rightward shift, relocate sine key points and use periodicity to complete each curve within the fixed domain.

questions.mappingNote: The horizontal-shift explanation gives the sign and direction of each translation.
questions.methodNote: Shift standard sine key points horizontally and retain the specified domain.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare sine curves with four different phase shifts.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret each internal addition as a leftward shift, relocate cosine key points and recover the portions needed to cover the fixed domain.

questions.mappingNote: Applies the horizontal-shift rule to cosine with negative h in the source's x−h notation.
questions.methodNote: Translate cosine key points left for a positive constant inside the angle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare cosine curves translated horizontally to the left.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert each frequency multiplier into a period and quarter-cycle spacing, then repeat the sine pattern across the specified interval.

questions.mappingNote: The changing-period discussion and Example 1(d) support plotting several cycles.
questions.methodNote: Use period 2π/n and repeated quarter-cycle sine values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare four sine periods on a common restricted domain.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine each cosine period from its frequency multiplier, position quarter-cycle key points and repeat the pattern to the domain endpoint.

questions.mappingNote: The period rule applies explicitly to cosine; Example 1(c) demonstrates a cosine frequency change.
questions.methodNote: Use period 2π/n and cosine quarter-cycle values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare four cosine periods on a common domain.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate amplitude, reflection, translation and period changes to place key points within each restricted domain, including shifted endpoints and partial cycles. These are linked applications of the taught sketching method.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–f use vertical/horizontal shifts and reflections; g–k additionally change period, with restricted domains determining the number of cycles.
questions.methodNote: Follow Example 1: amplitude, average, maximum, minimum, period, then transformed key points and a smooth sketch.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine dilations, reflections, translations and restricted domains.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine the denominator's range from cosine extrema, then recognise that its positive reciprocal is greatest at the smallest denominator.

questions.mappingNote: The amplitude and average method bounds the denominator; a positive reciprocal is largest at the smallest denominator.
questions.methodNote: Use cosine maximum/minimum and transformed range.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the cosine range to find an extremum of a positive reciprocal.

classification.difficultyReason: Account for the negative sine coefficient when finding denominator extrema, then select the largest positive denominator to minimise the reciprocal.

questions.mappingNote: The amplitude/average method gives the denominator range, then reciprocal order gives its minimum.
questions.methodNote: Use sine extrema to bound the transformed denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the sine range to minimise a positive reciprocal.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch both standard curves, use their phase relationship or equal-value angles to locate both intersections, and obtain exact ordinates with the correct signs.

questions.mappingNote: The sine/cosine graphs and their phase relationship support the graphical intersection method.
questions.methodNote: Sketch standard curves from key points and use symmetry to locate equal ordinates.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Sketch two curves and identify exact intersection coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Transform tangent zeros, asymptotes and branch directions, distinguish undefined endpoints from finite ones, and find new intercepts after vertical translations using standard tangent angles.

questions.mappingNote: a is standard tangent; b reflects; c changes period without reflection; d/e translate horizontally; f/g translate vertically, with g also reflected.
questions.methodNote: Use tangent period, zeros and vertical asymptotes; transform branches as in Example 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Transform tangent curves while preserving asymptotes and restricted-domain endpoints.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the mean, signed amplitude and period from four supplied transformed sine and cosine graphs.

questions.mappingNote: Question 14(a–d) directly repeats the sine/cosine rule-finding task in Example 3 on printed page 85. The 19F band occurs below these questions, so question 14 continues 19E.
questions.methodNote: Use maximum and minimum to find amplitude and average; use the initial direction or cosine starting value to determine the sign of a; equate the observed period to 2π/n.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read the mean, signed amplitude and period from four supplied transformed sine and cosine graphs.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise without a supplied route that tangency means an extremal vertical difference, then reframe sine minus cosine as a unit-circle line condition to derive both limiting translations and verify unique contact.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks for a graphical tangency condition between sine and a vertically translated cosine; graphical trigonometric equations is the closest directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: The inspected teaching introduces sine and cosine through unit-circle coordinates and describes vertical translations. The solution interprets the vertical gap using those coordinates and tangential contact, without calculus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine the two vertical translations giving a single tangential contact, using the extrema of the difference between sine and cosine.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine a cosine model from a graph, convert time units and solve for repeated heights over the ride.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 applies the same height-modelling method to a ferris wheel, then evaluates and solves the resulting model.
questions.methodNote: The clock example uses mean height, amplitude, initial position and period=2π/n to construct cosine models.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine a cosine model from a graph, convert time units and solve for repeated heights over the ride.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest demand is translating maximum survivable exposure into a four-hour interval centred on low tide, then evaluating depth at its endpoints. This connects a continuous duration constraint to a limiting height; the task also requires identifying missing clock-time information.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 extends periodic-height modelling to tides and continuous exposure. Model-periodic-phenomena is the closest skill for the complete task. The supplied teaching page contains the example prompt but not its worked demonstration.
questions.methodNote: The inspected Example 1 uses sine/cosine models for periodic heights. Use mean position, amplitude, starting position and period; solve level crossings with cosine angles and symmetry.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs a tidal model, solves repeated level crossings and interprets a maximum continuous exposure interval.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine the mean, amplitude and full period from temperature extrema six months apart, with time starting at the maximum.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 asks for a cosine model from a maximum, minimum and time between them, directly matching find-sinusoidal-model.
questions.methodNote: The inspected section introduction and clock Example 1 establish modelling periodic quantities with sine and cosine. Use the mean position, amplitude, period and initial position to select a cosine model.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Determine the mean, amplitude and full period from temperature extrema six months apart, with time starting at the maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine the mean, amplitude and angular frequency, then choose the cosine sign from the initial low tide.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 directly assesses finding a sinusoidal model from a minimum, maximum, period and initial position; find-sinusoidal-model is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 introduces cosine models for periodic heights using a fixed centre height, hand length as amplitude and rotation time as period. Use the corresponding mean-height, amplitude and period method for the tide.
